title: CASE OF KIRÁLY AND DÖMÖTÖR v. HUNGARY
conclusion: Violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8 - Positive obligations;Article 8-1 - Respect for private life);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
summary:
In the case of Király and Dömötör v. Hungary, the applicants, Mr. János Király and Mr. Tamás Dömötör, both of Roma origin, brought a complaint against Hungary concerning their treatment during and after an anti-Roma demonstration in Devecser. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller communities to racist intimidation and the failure of state authorities to protect them from hate-motivated threats and violence. On 5 August 2012, following tensions between Roma and non-Roma residents, a demonstration was organised by far-right groups and attended by hundreds, including members of Jobbik and other extremist organisations. The event featured inflammatory speeches inciting hatred against Roma, followed by a march through the Roma neighbourhood where demonstrators shouted death threats, racist insults, and threw stones and concrete at Roma homes. Despite a significant police presence, the authorities failed to intervene effectively or investigate the threats and violence adequately.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects the right to respect for private and family life. The Court found that Hungary had violated Article 8 by failing to provide adequate protection and to investigate the applicants’ complaints, awarding them non-pecuniary damages. This judgment is significant as it highlights the ongoing risks faced by Roma and Traveller communities in Europe and reinforces the obligation of states to actively protect minorities from hate-driven intimidation and violence, a persistent issue in the region’s recent history.
